post.body:
Do You Need a Road Maintenance Agreement?

If you’re buying land in a rural part of Colorado, the road to your future home might be private or shared. That means it’s not maintained by the county—and you may need a road maintenance agreement to satisfy lenders, ensure access, and avoid disputes down the line.

What Is a Road Maintenance Agreement?

It’s a legal document that outlines who is responsible for maintaining a private or shared road. These agreements typically cover:

  • Gravel grading and snow removal
  • Cost-sharing among neighbors
  • Access rights for emergency vehicles
  • Responsibility for repairs

Why Lenders Require It

Mortgage lenders and title companies want to ensure:

  • The road will be maintained and usable year-round
  • No future legal disputes will restrict access
  • You can get in and out during emergencies or winter months
Most lenders require a signed and recorded road maintenance agreement for any parcel accessed by a private or non-county road.

Common Issues Without One

  • Neighbors refusing to pay for repairs or plowing
  • Degraded road conditions making access difficult or impossible
  • Insurance issues and liability concerns in case of accidents

What Should Be Included?

  • Maintenance schedule (annually, seasonally, etc.)
  • Cost allocation method (equal shares, by frontage, etc.)
  • Process for decision-making and conflict resolution
  • Signatures of all current landowners involved

Final Advice

Never assume a road is maintained just because it looks drivable. Always check your title work and ensure your agent or attorney verifies the existence and validity of any road agreements.
